Cats: A cat has 230 bones in its body. A human has 206. A cat has no collarbone, so it can fit through any opening the size of its head.
Cats: Cats are extremely sensitive to vibrations. Cats are said to detect earthquake tremors 10 or 15 minutes before humans can.
Cats: Most cats give birth to a litter of between one and nine kittens. The largest known litter ever produced was 19 kittens, of which 15 survived.
Cats: The first commercially cloned pet was a cat named "Little Nicky." He cost his owner $50,000, making him one of the most expensive cats ever.
Cats: The smallest wildcat today is the Black-footed cat. The females are less than 20 inches (50 cm) long and can weigh as little as 2.5 lbs (1.2 kg).
Cats: On average, cats spend 2/3 of every day sleeping. That means a nine-year-old cat has been awake for only three years of its life.
Cats: A cat’s back is extremely flexible because it has up to 53 loosely fitting vertebrae. Humans only have 34.
Cats: Most cats had short hair until about 100 years ago, when it became fashionable to own cats and experiment with breeding.

Carrots were originally purple — the orange variety we know today was developed in the Netherlands in the 17th century.
Coffee beans are not beans, botanically — they are the seeds of a fruit called the coffee cherry.
The total length of the blood vessels in an adult human body, laid end to end, would circle the equator more than twice.
The world’s quietest room is at Microsoft’s headquarters in Redmond and measures –20.35 dBA — quieter than the limit of human hearing.
There are more theoretical chess games than there are atoms in the observable universe — Shannon’s number is about 10^120.
More than 1,000 species of fish, including some sharks, can change sex during their lifetime.
The longest word in major English dictionaries is the chemical name “pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis,” at 45 letters.
If you could fold a piece of standard paper 42 times, it would reach the Moon.
An adult human is made up of about 30 trillion cells, plus a roughly equal number of microbial cells.
There are more stars in the observable universe than there are grains of sand on every beach on Earth — by a wide margin.
The aglet is the small plastic or metal sheath at the end of a shoelace.
The vibrating black-and-yellow flight stripes used on some military runways were inspired by patterns observed on bees.
The dot above the lowercase letter “j” is also called a tittle.
The deepest part of the ocean ever recorded — Challenger Deep — is so far below sea level that the pressure is over a thousand times what we feel at the surface.
Cashews grow on the bottom of a fruit called a cashew apple, with the nut hanging like a single comma beneath each fruit.
Caffeine is the most widely used psychoactive substance in the world.
There’s a species of jellyfish (Turritopsis dohrnii) that can revert to its juvenile form, making it biologically immortal in principle.
The shortest reign in history was that of Louis-Antoine of France, who was technically king for about 20 minutes in 1830 between his father’s abdication and his own.
The strongest material currently known is graphene, a single layer of carbon atoms — about 200 times stronger by weight than steel.
About 100 billion neurons make up the human brain — roughly the same number as stars in the Milky Way galaxy.
The first email was sent in 1971 by Ray Tomlinson; he chose the @ symbol to separate user from machine because it was rarely used in text.
Mosquitoes are attracted to people who have recently exercised, partly because of the lactic acid in their sweat.
Fingernails grow about four times faster than toenails.
An ostrich’s eye is bigger than its brain.
Honeybees can recognize individual human faces and remember them for several days.
The plastic tip of a shoelace is called an aglet — and the tradition of using a hard tip dates back at least to Roman times.
Vanilla flavor is one of the most labor-intensive crops to harvest: each flower must be hand-pollinated within hours of opening.
An average bolt of lightning carries about a billion volts.
Wood frogs in North America can survive being frozen solid in winter; their hearts stop, then resume in spring.
Stainless steel was developed in 1913 in Sheffield, England, when Harry Brearley was looking for a corrosion-resistant gun-barrel alloy.
Ravens and crows can solve multi-step puzzles, recognize themselves in mirrors, and remember human faces for years.
The smell of fresh-cut grass is actually a chemical distress signal released by the grass.
Wi-Fi was developed from radio-astronomy techniques originally designed to detect black holes.
Grand Central Terminal in New York City has more platforms than any other train station in the world: 44 platforms and 67 tracks.
There are roughly four times as many bacterial cells in your body as there are human cells.
If you placed Saturn in a giant bathtub, it would float — its average density is less than that of water.
Greenland sharks may live for over 400 years, making them among the longest-living vertebrates known.
The Hubble Space Telescope orbits at about 540 km up, completing one orbit of Earth every 95 minutes.
The world’s first national park, Yellowstone, was established by the United States in 1872, before Wyoming was even a state.
Pythagoras of Samos, the mathematician, also led a religious-like community whose followers were forbidden to eat beans.
There’s no scientific consensus on why we yawn — leading hypotheses involve brain temperature regulation and social signaling.
Most modern violins still use the basic shape and proportions established by Italian luthiers like Stradivari in the 17th and 18th centuries.

words.def: A plant related to the thistle with enlarged flower heads eaten as a vegetable while immature, Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus.
The pleasant earthy scent produced when rain falls on dry soil.
words.example: The first rain of summer brought a wave of petrichor through the open windows.

words.def: The realization that each random passerby is living a life as vivid and complex as your own.
words.example: Walking through the airport, she was overwhelmed by a sudden wave of sonder.

words.def: The warmth of the sun in winter.
words.example: He stepped outside to enjoy a few minutes of apricity before returning to work.

words.def: Denoting a period of time in the past that was idyllically happy and peaceful.
words.example: She often spoke of her halcyon days as a graduate student.

words.def: Pleasingly smooth and musical to hear; sweet-sounding.
words.example: Her mellifluous voice carried easily across the auditorium.

words.def: Lasting for a very short time.
words.example: The beauty of cherry blossoms is famously ephemeral.

words.def: The occurrence of pleasant or beneficial events by chance.
words.example: Their meeting at the conference was pure serendipity.

words.def: Composure or coolness, especially under strain.
words.example: The pilot’s sangfroid during the emergency reassured every passenger.

words.def: The appearance of being true or real.
words.example: The novel’s details lent it remarkable verisimilitude.

words.def: The act of throwing something or someone out of a window.
words.example: The 1618 defenestration of Prague helped trigger the Thirty Years’ War.

words.def: A state of human flourishing or well-being, central to Aristotelian ethics.
words.example: For Aristotle, eudaimonia was the highest good a person could pursue.

words.def: The partially shaded outer region of a shadow cast by an opaque object.
words.example: During the eclipse, observers in the penumbra saw only a partial dimming.

words.def: A whispering, murmuring, or rustling sound.
words.example: A soft susurrus of leaves accompanied them along the path.

words.def: The state of being infatuated with another person, typically marked by intrusive thinking and craving for reciprocation.
words.example: Psychologists distinguish limerence from mature love.

words.def: Representing the most perfect or typical example of a quality or class.
words.example: Mozart’s G-minor symphony is a quintessential example of late Classical style.

words.def: Bubbly, lively, and enthusiastic.
words.example: Her effervescent personality lit up the meeting.

words.def: A fine, filmy substance, like cobwebs, found floating in the air or spread among grass.
words.example: Threads of gossamer drifted across the morning meadow.

words.def: Of or occurring every day; ordinary or everyday.
words.example: The diary recorded the quotidian rhythms of village life.

words.def: The lowest point in the fortunes of a person or organization.
words.example: The 2008 crisis marked the nadir of the firm’s revenue.

words.def: The highest point reached by a celestial or other object; the point of culmination.
words.example: The civilization reached its zenith in the third century.

words.def: An unfilled space; a gap, especially in a manuscript or argument.
words.example: The historian noted a lacuna in the records covering the 1340s.

words.def: A manuscript or surface on which later writing has been superimposed on effaced earlier writing.
words.example: The medieval text turned out to be a palimpsest concealing an older Greek work.

words.def: Characterized by long words; long-winded.
words.example: His sesquipedalian style made the report unnecessarily difficult to read.

words.def: Having an obstinately uncooperative attitude.
words.example: The recalcitrant printer refused to acknowledge the new driver.

words.def: Too great or extreme to be expressed in words.
words.example: She felt an ineffable sadness as she watched the train pull away.

words.def: The view that the self is all that can be known to exist.
words.example: The argument quickly slid into philosophical solipsism.

words.def: Relating to knowledge or to the degree of its validation.
words.example: There is an epistemic difference between believing and knowing.

words.def: Enabling someone to discover or learn something for themselves; using a practical, often imperfect method.
words.example: The team adopted a heuristic approach to triage incoming bug reports.

words.def: Knowing or using several languages.
words.example: Working in international finance, she became thoroughly polyglot.

words.def: Intended for or likely to be understood by only a small number of people with specialized knowledge.
words.example: The esoteric details of the regulation tripped up newer staff.

words.def: Occupying a position at, or on both sides of, a boundary or threshold.
words.example: Airports are liminal spaces — neither here nor there.

words.def: Mental calmness and composure, especially in a difficult situation.
words.example: She handled the criticism with surprising equanimity.

words.def: Carried out with a minimum of effort or reflection.
words.example: He gave the report a perfunctory glance before signing it.

words.def: Clear, logical, and convincing.
words.example: She made a cogent argument for restructuring the team.

words.def: Stated or appearing to be true, but not necessarily so.
words.example: The ostensible reason for the meeting was logistics, but everyone sensed something else was up.

words.def: A person who acts obsequiously toward someone important in order to gain advantage.
words.example: The CEO surrounded himself with sycophants and paid the price.

words.def: Not likely to provoke dissent or offense; bland.
words.example: The press release was deliberately anodyne.

words.def: Larger or more generous than is usual or necessary.
words.example: The university received a munificent gift from an anonymous alumna.

words.def: Having a particular habit, activity, or interest that is long-established and unlikely to change.
words.example: He was an inveterate reader who finished a book a week.

words.def: Most noticeable or important.
words.example: Let me summarize the salient points of the proposal.

words.def: Present, appearing, or found everywhere.
words.example: Smartphones have become ubiquitous in modern life.

words.def: Having a harmful effect, especially in a gradual or subtle way.
words.example: The pernicious influence of misinformation can be hard to undo.

words.def: Providing psychological relief through the open expression of strong emotions.
words.example: Writing the letter, even unsent, was deeply cathartic.

words.def: Fluent or persuasive in speaking or writing.
words.example: Her eloquent speech moved the audience to applause.

words.def: Dealing with things sensibly and realistically, in a practical way.
words.example: His pragmatic approach kept the project on schedule.

words.def: Looking or sounding sad and dismal.
words.example: The basset hound watched her leave with lugubrious eyes.

words.def: Cheerful and full of energy.
words.example: The team was ebullient after the surprise victory.

words.def: Showing a lack of courage or determination; timid.
words.example: His pusillanimous refusal to speak up cost the team dearly.

words.def: Having a ready insight into and understanding of things.
words.example: The perspicacious editor caught problems no one else had noticed.

words.def: Tending to induce drowsiness or sleep.
words.example: The lecturer’s monotone delivery had a soporific effect.

words.def: Eager or quick to argue or fight; aggressively defiant.
words.example: The negotiations stalled when one side turned truculent.

words.def: Subject to sudden or unpredictable changes of mood or mind.
words.example: His mercurial temperament made him hard to manage.

words.def: Optimistic or positive, especially in an apparently bad situation.
words.example: Despite the setback, she remained sanguine about the project’s prospects.

words.def: Unclear, vague, or ill-defined.
words.example: The proposal was rejected for being too nebulous.

words.def: Unable to be resisted or avoided; inescapable.
words.example: The ineluctable conclusion is that we need to start over.

words.def: To find out for certain; to make sure of.
words.example: Investigators are working to ascertain the cause of the outage.

words.def: To make less severe, serious, or painful.
words.example: Sandbags helped mitigate the worst of the flooding.

words.def: To promote or make widely known (an idea or cause); to put a law into effect.
words.example: The new policy was promulgated to all branch offices.

words.def: To deliberately make something unclear or harder to understand.
words.example: The contract’s wording seemed designed to obfuscate the fees.

words.def: To cease resisting an opponent or an unwelcome demand; to surrender.
words.example: After hours of arguing, she finally capitulated.

words.def: A change of circumstances or fortune, typically one that is unwelcome.
words.example: She faced the vicissitudes of life with steady humor.
